Packaging July 8, 2026

# Anyscale stops publishing H100 and H200 rates; newer GPUs are now quote-only

Anyscale pricing

Anyscale still bills instance-hours in its own credits, but it no longer tells you what a Hopper GPU costs. The new row covers Hopper, Blackwell and Grace-Blackwell parts, so every accelerator newer than the A100 now needs a sales conversation.

What it means for buyers. If you run small or mid-sized Ray workloads on CPU, T4, L4, A10G or A100 instances, nothing changes: those rates are public and you can try them on the $100 starter credit. If you need H100s or newer, you can no longer estimate the bill from the website or compare it with GPU clouds that publish hourly rates; budget for a quote, and use committed-usage terms (Anyscale offers volume discounts on prepaid usage) as your negotiating lever. The old public H100 rate (AC 9.2880 an hour) is a reference point for that negotiation.

What it means for the market. Anyscale pulled the rates weeks before Nscale, a GPU cloud that owns its own data centers, agreed to buy it on 30 July. Neither company has linked the two, so read it as an order of events, not a cause.

results.title: The Self-Hosted GPU Breakeven Point: Why ~50M Tokens/Day Is Where Owning H100s Beats Renting Inference APIs | bex.co
highlights:
The self-hosted side is a fixed cost. Dedicated H100 SXM capacity from a GPU cloud (Lambda Labs, RunPod, CoreWeave, or a neocloud reseller) has stabilized in 2026 in the $2.85–$3.50/hour range for reserved capacity, with outliers like Hyperbolic advertising lows near $1.49/hour and hyperscaler on-demand pricing running $4–$11/hour. Take $3.00/hour as a representative dedicated rate: run it 24/7 and that's $2,190/month, or about $72/day — a number that doesn't move whether the GPU serves one request or ten thousand. (Buying the card outright tells the same story from a different angle: an H100 PCIe runs $25,000–$31,000 and an SXM5 unit $35,000–$40,000+, and once you amortize that over three years and add the power, cooling, and facilities overhead that owning bare metal requires — commonly cited at 2.5–3x the raw hardware cost — a purchased card converges on roughly the same $2,500–$3,500/month all-in figure as renting dedicated capacity. Ownership only pulls ahead of renting past 10,000+ GPU-hours/month sustained for multiple years, which is a data-center operator's math, not a single team's.)

...

This is the load-bearing insight for a self-hosted PaaS weighing "give every tenant its own GPU" against "proxy every tenant to a hosted API": neither extreme is right. A single tenant's traffic essentially never clears the utilization needed to make a dedicated card pencil out — but a platform that bin-packs many tenants' AI-agent sandboxes onto shared, owned GPU-node capacity can realistically sustain 70-90% utilization across the pool, the range where self-hosting stops being a bet and starts being the obviously cheaper option against everything but the rock-bottom budget tier. The GPU-node capacity itself typically comes from dedicated neocloud instances (Lambda, RunPod, CoreWeave, Hyperbolic) or owned bare metal rather than Hetzner specifically — Hetzner doesn't currently sell H100 SKUs — but the underlying economics (fixed-cost commodity hardware, amortized across pooled demand) are the same commodity-ownership logic Hetzner made popular for CPU nodes, now applied to GPUs.

results.title: What does a GPU actually cost to run? | Lucas Zelko
highlights:
What does a GPU actually cost to run?

Most pricing stops at the rental rate. But the real cost of an accelerator has three parts: what you pay to rent it, what it costs to power, and the carbon it puts out. We now publish all three observed, per SKU, across 40+ marketplaces, updated daily.

A snapshot from today's data:

H100 SXM - $2.50/GPU-hr · $0.050/hr power · 43 gCO₂e/hr (FI grid)
H200 SXM - $4.39/GPU-hr · $0.161/hr power · 258 gCO₂e/hr (DE grid)
A100 SXM 80GB - $1.86/GPU-hr · $0.045/hr power · 30 gCO₂e/hr (FR grid)
RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell - $2.06/GPU-hr · $0.136/hr power · 244 gCO₂e/hr (CZ grid)
RTX 4090 - $0.65/GPU-hr · $0.082/hr power · 205 gCO₂e/hr (BG grid)

One thing worth reading twice: carbon varies more by *where* a chip runs than by the chip itself. An H100 in Finland and an H200 in Germany look worlds apart on emissions, that's the grid, not the silicon.

Location is now a first-order variable in compute cost.

Every figure here is observed, not modeled. Where we don't have clean data, we publish nothing rather than an estimate.

We're an independent reference.

Just the numbers.

results.title: GPU Rental Rates by Generation: Nine Years of Posted Prices · CCIR Research
highlights:
Basis Posted panel-median guaranteed on-demand rate, $/GPU-hr, monthly, log scale, Oct 2017 – Apr 2026 (the archive's edge — one uniform right edge for every generation; the live CCIR panel continues from there). Solid lines are a centered 3-month rolling median (display smoothing only — fits, labels, and the table below are computed on the raw monthly medians, drawn as the faint steps). Step-function repair: posted prices carry forward between captures. Shaded bands are the two demand episodes described in §02.

...

| Generation | Window (n≥3) | Log-linear fit | Less CPI | R² | Endpoint CAGR | Median, first → last |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V100 | Jun 2019 – Apr 2026 (6.8y) | −15.3%/yr | −19.2%/yr | 0.82 | −15.9%/yr | $2.69 → $0.82 |
| A100 | Sep 2021 – Apr 2026 (4.6y) | no clear trend | no clear trend | 0.05 | +4.6%/yr | $2.20 → $2.70 |
| H100 | Sep 2023 – Apr 2026 (2.6y) | −15.3%/yr | −18.4%/yr | 0.57 | +1.5%/yr | $3.50 → $3.64 |

 V100 and H100 declined about 15% a year. A100 shows no clear trend. Twice in nine years, demand for compute outran the supply of chips, and posted rates rose on generations that were already several years old (§02). V100, the one generation observable from mid-life to end-of-life, declined as fast as H100 and most regularly. A100's posted median was $2.20 in September 2021, peaked at $3.05 in 2022, fell to $1.70 in late 2024, and ended at $2.70 in April 2026, +4.6% per year endpoint to endpoint. H100's posted median also ends the window higher than it began it.

...

## 02 Two Demand Episodes

 The decline has been interrupted twice, visibly, in nine years. 

 2021–2023. Posted rates on then-current and prior generations firmed through the GPU shortage and the first phase of the AI buildout. V100, four to six years old, rose 48% at DataCrunch and was repriced upward at OVHcloud. A100 rates at the repricers rose through 2023 into early 2024, and Lambda raised its A100 list prices outright in January 2024. The episode ended in mid-2024: A100 and V100 posted rates stepped down 30–56% from their peaks over the following year. 

 Late 2025 – the window's edge. The declines bottomed between late 2024 and August 2025. From roughly December 2025, posted rates turned up across every generation still listed, at every provider that reprices, driven by demand from the AI buildout: H100 +29% at Verda by December, H200 +70% by March. In spring 2026 Lambda raised A100 by 56% in seven weeks and repriced V100, silicon approaching its ninth year, from a list unchanged since June 2022. The sticky tier, as in the first episode, has not moved. This is the sharpest broad repricing of prior-generation silicon in the record.

...

Guaranteed on-demand rates only: reserved, interruptible (hyperscaler "Spot" products and community tiers alike), and "starting-at" teaser rows are excluded. USD only. Per-instance prices are divided to per-GPU with the derivation recorded per row. Known page bugs are excluded.

results.title: Most firms building AI infrastructure cost models are using the wrong numbers. | Vasilij Nevlev
highlights:
Most firms building AI infrastructure cost models are using the wrong numbers.

They’re quoting hyperscaler list prices for GPU compute.

Current on-demand H100 rates from specialist GPU clouds: $1.50–$2 per hour.

Hyperscaler list prices for the same hardware: $5–$11 per hour.

That’s a 50–80% gap - and it’s not a negotiated discount, it’s the standard market rate on specialist platforms that most enterprise procurement processes don’t reach.

Why this matters right now:

The “rent a frontier model vs run it locally” calculation is heavily influenced by compute cost. If you’re using hyperscaler pricing in that model, you’re overstating the cost of the rented-GPU option by a significant margin.

Thunder Compute tracks on-demand H100 and A100 pricing across 15+ cloud providers monthly. It’s the reference to use before building a business case around GPU costs - rather than quoting a number that was stale before the spreadsheet was finished.

The practical implication: for teams evaluating whether rented compute is viable for a specific workload, the specialist cloud rate is the relevant comparison - not the AWS or Azure list price.

# 2026 GPU Rental Prices Fall, Practical Guide for Small Teams Deploying Inference

 2026-07-08 275 

Rental prices for high-end cards like the Nvidia B200 have dropped more than 30% from recent highs, giving many small teams and individual developers an opportunity to deploy AI inference services. Over the past six months, training demand has driven up overall compute costs; now that prices are easing, it's a good time to focus more on inference optimization.

In practice, first assess your model size and concurrency requirements. For lightweight text generation or simple classification tasks, a single 4090 or A100 can handle the load; for video understanding or multimodal inference, multi-card parallelism is needed. Rental platforms typically offer hourly or monthly billing, so it's advisable to start with a small test environment for a few days, observe actual throughput and latency, and then decide on scaling.

...

There are several practical cost-saving tips. During the price drop, prioritize locking in monthly or quarterly plans, which can save an additional 15-25% compared to hourly billing. Also, enable idle card reclamation to release resources immediately after tasks finish, avoiding full-card charges. A university research group did this: they used rental services to get nearly 300 independent environments at once, students called resources on demand, deployment time dropped from several days to a few hours, and overall costs stayed within budget.

A common mistake is to only look at single-card prices and ignore network and storage. Inference services are latency-sensitive; when choosing nodes, prioritize data centers in the same region or with high-speed interconnects. For projects with large data volumes, pay attention to object storage costs—placing models and vector databases in the same availability zone can save cross-region traffic fees.

...

Price drops don't mean permanently low prices; keep an eye on platform announcements and market trends weekly. Once demand for new cards like the B200 picks up, prices could rebound quickly. Stock up on common images and configuration scripts in advance so you can quickly switch card types or nodes when volatility hits.

NexGpu offers an elastic GPU pool for such scenarios, supporting seamless scaling from single-card testing to multi-card clusters. Users can flexibly adjust based on actual usage without long-term commitment. In real projects, many teams have used it for medical imaging inference and financial risk models, with good feedback on stability and ease of use.

highlights:
# 全球GPU服务器告急：截至9月容量订满，H100租价涨40%

 2026-07-08 15:07:35 分享到 

2026年初，试图在市场上租用GPU服务器算力，已经变得像抢购热门演唱会门票一样困难：价格高企，且几乎无货。

专注芯片与AI基础设施研究的权威机构SemiAnalysis发布的深度报告揭示，当前全球GPU算力租用市场正经历史无前例的供需失衡。无论是H100、H200，还是最新一代Blackwell架构的B200，可租用容量已全面告罄。更令人震惊的是，截至2026年8至9月的所有新增部署容量，均已被提前预订完毕。

### H100租价暴涨40%：供不应求的最直接证明 

2025年10月，一份一年期H100 GPU租用合同的价格约为1.70美元/GPU·小时。然而，到了2026年1月底，这一价格已突破2美元大关，并在2月至3月间继续月环比上涨15–20%，最终在3月达到约2.35美元/GPU·小时——涨幅接近40%。

这一趋势完全颠覆了此前行业的普遍预期。市场原本认为：随着英伟达Blackwell架构新品上市，H100作为上一代产品，其租用价格应当逐步下降。然而现实恰恰相反——H100不仅没有降价，反而比新品更紧俏。

已持有H100租约的客户，面对价格飙升，宁可支付高昂续费也不愿放弃手中的算力。市场上甚至出现了"算力二房东"现象：部分持有GPU集群租约的机构，开始将手中的算力像分租公寓一样转租给其他买家，以期从中套利。

### Blackwell同样难逃缺货 

理论上，新一代Blackwell GPU（B200、GB200）的上市应能缓解H100的压力。但实际情况是：Blackwell系列的新部署交货周期同样延伸至2026年6月至7月，且大量产能已被各大超大规模云厂商（亚马逊、微软、谷歌等）提前锁定，中小企业几乎难以获得分配。
